steps: Apply the operator with a scalar and print the result's length.
Square the array with ** and confirm every element changed.
Point at the operator, not a loop: the compiled pass visits all elements once.
Arithmetic is elementwise.realWorld: Converting a column of prices or rescaling a feature vector is one expression, so the code reads like the formula on the slide.
mistakes: Writing a for loop over the elements and paying interpreter cost per value.
Expecting the expression to change the array in place.
revision: Operators on arrays are universal functions applied element by element.
The shape is preserved and a new array is returned.

steps: Call each ufunc with a scalar to see the plain number it returns.
Pass an array instead and note the same call now returns an array.
Keep one spelling: the ufunc form works for both inputs.
Math ufuncs.realWorld: A helper written with np.sqrt works whether it receives a single measurement or a whole column, which is why libraries standardise on ufuncs.
mistakes: Importing math and using math.sqrt, which refuses an array.
Forgetting the dtype widens to float even for exact roots.
revision: ufuncs accept scalars, lists and arrays through one call.
The result dtype follows the computation, not the input.

steps: Compare the array with the threshold and print the boolean array.
Index the array with that mask to keep only the True positions.
Count with mask.sum() when only the number matters.
Comparisons produce masks.realWorld: Pass lists, outlier flags and alert counts are all one comparison away from the raw column.
mistakes: Writing if a > 2: on an array, which has no single truth value.
Assuming the filtered result keeps the original shape.
revision: Comparisons return a boolean array of the same shape.
Indexing with the mask shortens the array to the matches.

steps: Pass a list of perfect squares to np.sqrt.
Print the float array and check each value against the hand answer.
Note the dtype: the result is float even though every root is whole.
sqrt of perfect squares is exact.realWorld: Distances and standard deviations are roots of sums, so exact roots give a free way to check a numerical path.
mistakes: Expecting an integer dtype because the inputs were integers.
Comparing the float result with == instead of isclose.
revision: sqrt is a ufunc over the whole array in one compiled pass.
The output shape matches the input and the dtype is float.

steps: Fold a short array to a single total with reduce.
Return every intermediate total with accumulate.
Compare lengths: reduce gives one value, accumulate keeps the input length.
reduce sums, accumulate keeps running to.realWorld: A checkout total is reduce; a running balance chart is accumulate. Both come from the same ufunc method.
mistakes: Calling reduce on a matrix without an axis and flattening by accident.
Using a Python accumulator loop where accumulate already exists.
revision: reduce collapses to one value per axis.
accumulate keeps every intermediate result.

steps: Clip values below and above the range.
Print the result and confirm the in-range value is untouched.
Check the values that were pinned to each bound.
clip limits every element.realWorld: Keeping predicted probabilities inside [0, 1] and pixel channels inside [0, 255] is one clip, not a per-element if.
mistakes: Passing the bounds in the wrong order.
Clipping before a downstream sum that should have seen the raw values.
revision: clip pins values into a closed range.
Values already inside the range pass through unchanged.

steps: Apply all three to the same decimals.
Compare where 1.5 lands under each.
Pick the rule the data means before choosing the function.
round, floor and ceil differ.realWorld: Billing rounds to the nearest cent, stock planning floors to whole units, and page counts ceil — picking the wrong one changes the number of items.
mistakes: Assuming round always goes up at .5; it goes to the nearest even.
Using astype(int) as a rounding step — that truncates toward zero.
revision: round is half-to-even, floor always down, ceil always up.
astype(int) truncates, so it is not a rounding replacement.

steps: Apply sign to a mix of negative, zero and positive values.
Read the -1, 0 and 1 array as directions.
Multiply it into other data to flip only the negatives.
sign tells you direction.realWorld: Direction columns in time-series data — up, flat, down — come from sign, and multiplying by it separates gains from losses.
mistakes: Using sign when the magnitude is still needed.
Assuming NaN maps to 0; it propagates.
revision: sign returns -1, 0 or 1 elementwise.
It is a direction array, not a magnitude.

steps: Square an integer array with **.
Repeat with np.power and compare the values.
Note that both accept an array exponent, not only a scalar one.
Exponentiation uses the ** operator.realWorld: Polynomial features are powers of one column; ** keeps the expression readable while np.power is the form to pass as a callback.
mistakes: Using a negative integer exponent on an integer array and getting a ValueError.
Reading ** as matrix power; matrix power is np.linalg.matrix_power.
revision: ** is elementwise on arrays.
np.power is the same operation as a function.

steps: Pass an array with negatives to np.abs.
Print the result and confirm it is elementwise.
Try the same call with a plain Python list to see it accepts both.
abs works on whole arrays.realWorld: Residuals and error magnitudes are absolute values; a library that accepts arrays, lists and scalars keeps callers from converting first.
mistakes: Calling the Python builtin abs on a multi-element array.
Assuming abs changes the dtype when the input is unsigned.
revision: np.abs is a ufunc over the whole array.
One call serves scalars, lists and arrays.

steps: Cumulatively sum a short array.
Compare the last value with the plain total.
Note the output length equals the input length.
cumsum keeps every running total.visual:
np.cumsum([1 2 3]) → [1 3 6]
last value 6 = the plain sum
cumsum keeps every running total.realWorld: Running balances, cumulative sales targets and progress charts are cumsum; the collapsed total is a different question.
mistakes: Using cumsum where only the final total was wanted.
Forgetting the axis on a matrix and flattening it.
revision: cumsum returns an array of the same length.
sum collapses to one number instead.

steps: Take the log of positive values.
Exponentiate the result.
Compare with the original using np.allclose rather than ==.
log and exp invert each other.realWorld: Log-space transforms in modelling are only reversible if the round trip is checked within a tolerance, not with equality.
mistakes: Checking the round trip with == and calling the float error a bug.
Taking log(0), which yields -inf with a warning.
revision: exp and log are inverses up to floating-point error.
allclose is the correct comparison for that round trip.

steps: Fold a length-4 array to one number with reduce.
Produce every running total with accumulate.
Swap add for multiply and see the same two shapes.
reduce and accumulate.realWorld: Any binary ufunc gets these two methods for free, so a custom operator inherits totals and running totals without new code.
mistakes: Assuming the methods exist only on np.add.
Reducing a multi-dimensional array without naming the axis.
revision: reduce and accumulate are ufunc methods, not array-only helpers.
They reduce or run over the axis you name.

steps: Add 0.1 and 0.2 and compare with 0.3 using ==.
Repeat with np.isclose and see the difference.
Set rtol/atol when the tolerance needs to match the domain.
Never compare floats with ==.realWorld: Model checks and test assertions on floats fail on the last bits unless they compare within a tolerance — this is the standard fix.
mistakes: Using == in a test assertion on computed floats.
Choosing a tolerance so loose that a real error passes.
revision: Binary floats cannot represent most decimals exactly.
isclose and allclose compare within a tolerance.

steps: Add a scalar to a vector.
Print the result and confirm every element moved.
Note that no array of ten was allocated for the scalar.
Scalar broadcasting.realWorld: Adding a fixed fee or a currency offset to a whole column is one addition, and the memory cost does not grow with the row count.
mistakes: Building a full array of the constant first.
Assuming the scalar changes the dtype silently.
revision: A scalar broadcasts to every position without a copy.
The result shape is the array's shape.

steps: Build a (2, 3) matrix and a length-3 weight vector.
Multiply them and print the result.
Confirm each column was scaled by its own weight.
Row and column broadcasting.realWorld: Feature scaling multiplies each column by its own weight; that is the shape rule every preprocessing pipeline relies on.
mistakes: Aligning shapes from the left instead of the right.
Passing the weights as a column and scaling rows by mistake.
revision: Shapes align from the right.
A (3,) operand matches the last axis of a (2, 3).

Incompatible shapes fail loudly.syntax: a + b   # ValueError when sizes disagree
steps: Add two matrices whose last axes differ and neither is 1.
Catch the ValueError and read the two shapes it prints.
Fix the axis rather than reshaping until the error stops.
Incompatible shapes fail loudly.visual:
(2, 3) + (2, 2)
→ ValueError: operands could not be broadcast
Incompatible shapes fail loudly.realWorld: A mismatched feature and weight vector is the most common preprocessing bug, and this error is the one that catches it before training.
mistakes: Reshaping blindly until the error disappears.
Blaming the data instead of the shapes printed in the message.
revision: Sizes must be equal or one on every aligned axis.
The error names both shapes — read it right to left.

steps: Build a (2, 3) matrix of ones.
Add a length-3 row vector.
Print the result and confirm both rows received the same addition.
A vector broadcasts across rows.realWorld: Subtracting a per-column mean from every row uses exactly this stretch, which is why column statistics are length-n vectors.
mistakes: Expecting a different offset per row from a 1-D vector.
Mismatching the column count and reading the error as a row problem.
revision: A (n,) operand is treated as one row repeated per matrix row.
The column count must match exactly.

steps: Build a (2, 3) matrix and a (2, 1) column.
Add them and print the result.
Confirm each row shifted by its own value.
A column broadcasts down.realWorld: Normalising each sample by its own total — a per-row operation — needs the divisor as a (m, 1) column.
mistakes: Encoding the per-row value as a flat (2,) vector, which aligns with columns instead.
Forgetting keepdims when the column came from a reduction.
revision: A (m, 1) column stretches across every column of the matrix.
The row count must match.

steps: Add a trailing axis to the first vector and a leading axis to the second.
Multiply them and print the (2, 2) table.
Check one cell by hand against the pair it should combine.
Outer product uses two new axes.realWorld: Pairwise interaction features and distance tables are outer products; they replace a nested loop over both vectors.
mistakes: Leaving both operands 1-D and getting a dot product instead.
Using the wrong slot for the new axis and transposing the table.
revision: One new axis per operand makes broadcasting compute every pair.
The result shape is (len(a), len(b)).

steps: Build a matrix and compute its per-column mean.
Compare the matrix with that length-3 vector.
Print the boolean matrix and confirm one comparison per row.
Comparison broadcasts too.visual:
mean(axis=0) → [4.5 3. 3.]
a > mean → [[False False False]
            [ True  True  True]]
Comparison broadcasts too.realWorld: Flagging values above their own column average is one broadcast comparison, not a loop over columns.
mistakes: Assuming broadcasting works only for arithmetic.
Comparing against a (2, 1) mean and getting a transposed mask.
revision: Every ufunc broadcasts, including comparisons.
The mask has the broadcast shape.

steps: Reshape a length-3 vector into a (3, 1) column.
Add a (1, 2) row of zeros to it.
Print the shape and confirm it is (3, 2).
reshape prepares a strip for broadcastin.realWorld: Building a grid of coordinates or a pairwise table starts by giving each operand the axis it is missing.
mistakes: Reshaping to (3,) and expecting the outer grid.
Adding the operands in the wrong orientation.
revision: Each operand contributes the axes it has.
Length-1 axes stretch to the other operand's size.

steps: Add a length-3 vector to a (2, 3) matrix.
Print the result's shape and confirm it is still (2, 3).
Note that the vector was never copied into two rows.
A row array broadcasts across rows.realWorld: Centering every column uses this stretch, which is why a scaler stores a length-n mean rather than a full matrix.
mistakes: Expecting the result to grow a row.
Mismatching the last axis and reading the ValueError as a rank problem.
revision: A (n,) operand matches the last axis.
The output keeps the matrix's shape.

steps: Multiply a matrix by a scalar.
Print the values and confirm all four changed.
Note that the shape is unchanged.
A scalar is the smallest broadcast.realWorld: Unit conversions across a whole table are one scalar multiplication, and the cost does not depend on the table size.
mistakes: Looping over cells for a constant operation.
Assuming the multiplication edited the matrix in place.
revision: A scalar has no axes, so nothing can misalign.
The result is a new array of the same shape.

steps: Multiply a (2, 1) column by a (2,) row.
Print the (2, 2) result.
Verify each cell is one row value times one column value.
Broadcast a column against a row.realWorld: Every pairwise combination — price × quantity, user × item — is this one line instead of a nested loop.
mistakes: Expecting elementwise pairing from a column and a row.
Confusing the (2, 2) grid with a dot product.
revision: A column and a row broadcast into the full grid.
The result shape is the pair of lengths.

steps: Add a (3, 1) column of zeros to a length-4 vector.
Print the shape and confirm it is (3, 4).
Explain which axis stretched on each operand.
A size of one stretches automatically.realWorld: Grid construction and one-hot expansion both rely on length-1 axes stretching to the other operand's size.
mistakes: Assuming a length-1 axis must match a length-1 axis.
Forgetting that a missing axis is treated as length 1 too.
revision: A length-1 axis repeats to match the other operand.
This is why keepdims results broadcast straight back.

steps: Build a (3, 1) column and a (1, 4) row.
Add them and print the (3, 4) result.
Check a corner cell against the pair that produced it.
A column broadcasts against a row.realWorld: Adding a per-row offset to a per-column base — a table of shifts — is one addition once both are shaped correctly.
mistakes: Building the row as (4,) and the column as (3,) and losing the grid.
Broadcasting a (3,) against a (1, 4) and getting a shape error.
revision: Both length-1 axes stretch to the other operand's size.
The result combines every row with every column.

steps: Start with a length-3 vector.
Insert an axis at position 0 and print the shape.
Insert it at position 1 and compare (1, 3) with (3, 1).
expand_dims adds the axis explicitly.realWorld: Function pipelines cannot use the [:, None] syntax, so expand_dims is the form that survives being passed as a step in a chain.
mistakes: Choosing the wrong position and broadcasting the opposite direction.
Forgetting the axis argument is required.
revision: expand_dims is the function form of newaxis.
The position decides row versus column.
